study.title: Topographically Forced Stationary Waves Can Explain the Near-Surface Zonal Winds Observed by Huygens on Titan

cover.headline: **Titan's mountains may explain** why the Huygens probe measured winds blowing the wrong way when it landed

slides.title: Large-scale topography might create local wind patterns that contradict a moon's overall circulation.
slides.body:
Climate models consistently predict westward winds near Titan's surface. But Huygens measured eastward winds instead.

This early paper reports that mountains could force stationary waves that flip wind direction in some spots.

slides.title: The team paired two simulations of Titan's atmosphere: one with topography, one without.
slides.body:
Only the version with mountains reproduced the eastward flow Huygens saw in the lowest kilometer.

The effect comes from overlapping wave patterns locked to the terrain. A wave with one peak around the moon provides the eastward push.

slides.title: Titan's equator superrotates: the atmosphere spins faster than the surface beneath it.
slides.body:
That creates a westward wind at the ground everywhere, according to models. Huygens landed in 2005 and measured the opposite.

The team now argues that what Huygens saw was a local exception, not a problem with the models.

caveats: This is a preprint. It has not been peer reviewed, so no independent expert has checked the work yet.
This study found a pattern, not a cause. Something else could explain the link between terrain and wind direction.
The conclusions about why the probe measured eastward winds are our own extrapolation. Read the full paper for what the authors actually claim.

source.abstract: Titan's equatorial superrotation is associated with climatological retrograde (westward) near-surface winds at low latitudes, as consistently simulated by Titan general circulation models. However, the Huygens probe measured prograde (eastward) near-surface winds, contrary to the expected circulation. We investigate whether these observations reflect localized forcing by large-scale topography, using paired three-dimensional dry simulations with and without topography in the Titan Atmospheric Model. We find that topography generates longitude-locked, vertically structured zonal wind anomalies that reproduce key features of the Huygens wind profile in the lowest few kilometers. Helmholtz and spectral analyses show that this structure arises from the superposition of several vertically varying low wavenumber modes. A predominantly rotational, topographically forced stationary zonal wavenumber s=1 response provides a major eastward anomaly throughout the lowest 2 km, whereas a locally divergent s=4 response consistent with a gravity wave, opposes it near the surface. Weaker s=2 and s=3 responses also vary vertically and contribute eastward anomalies near the surface. Combined with the retrograde zonal-mean circulation, these modes produce a Huygens-like profile characterized by prograde flow within the lowest 1 km and shear toward retrograde flow aloft. The paired simulations establish their topographic origin, while coherence with the corresponding terrain-forcing components demonstrates that the responses remain phase locked to the forcing. Similar but weaker stationary responses are simulated near the planned Dragonfly landing site, providing baseline expectations for interpreting its future atmospheric measurements. This study demonstrates how large-scale topography can generate localized departures from Titan's zonal-mean circulation and highlights the importance of stationary waves.
